MUJAHID:v1p375/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v1p375/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v1p375/r1.claim: Mujahid glosses the dog's place at the cave's entrance as the courtyard.

MUQATIL:18:18-21/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:18:18-21/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:18:18-21/r1.claim: They look awake because their eyes are open while they are being turned over, although they are asleep.

MUQATIL:18:18-21/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:18:18-21/r2.speaker: الضحاك
MUQATIL:18:18-21/r2.claim: Al-Dahhak says Gabriel turned them twice each year so the earth would not consume their flesh.

MUQATIL:18:18-21/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:18:18-21/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:18:18-21/r3.claim: God turns the sleepers from one side to the other without their awareness.

MUQATIL:18:18-21/r4.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:18:18-21/r4.speaker: author
MUQATIL:18:18-21/r4.claim: The dog was called Qumṭīr, belonged to the shepherd Maksalmina, and lay with forelegs extended at the cave entrance to guard the youths.

MUQATIL:18:18-21/r5.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:18:18-21/r5.speaker: author
MUQATIL:18:18-21/r5.claim: God put the dog to sleep for those years as He put the youths to sleep; seeing them would make someone flee in terror.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p174#2/r5.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p174#2/r5.speaker: author
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p174#2/r5.claim: The sleepers look awake because their eyes are open, though they are dead.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p175/r1.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p175/r1.speaker: قتادة
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p175/r1.claim: Qatāda says the youths were turned from side to side during their first sleep, before they died; Abū ʿIyāḍ says this happened twice each year.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p175/r2.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p175/r2.speaker: قتادة
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p175/r2.claim: Qatāda places the dog's outstretched forelegs at the cave's entrance; seeing the sleepers would cause a visitor to flee in terror because of their condition.

FARRA:v2p137/r2.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v2p137/r2.speaker: author
FARRA:v2p137/r2.claim: Asim and al-A'mash read ولملئت lightly; Medina's readers double the ل; the address is to Muhammad.

FARRA:v2p137/r6.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v2p137/r6.speaker: author
FARRA:v2p137/r6.claim: يقظ and يقظ are both forms for the singular of أيقاظ.

MAJAZ:v1p396/r2.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p396/r2.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p396/r2.claim: Yaqiẓ is singular ayqāẓ; ayqāẓ may also be treated as the plural of yaqẓān.

MAJAZ:v1p396/r3.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p396/r3.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p396/r3.claim: Ruʾbah's verse uses ayqāẓ for people who are awake.

MAJAZ:v1p396/r4.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p396/r4.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p396/r4.claim: Nuqallibuhum means turning them over onto their right and left sides.

MAJAZ:v1p396/r5.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p396/r5.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p396/r5.claim: Waṣīd means the door or space before it; the door is shut, and its plurals are waṣāʾid and waṣd.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p399#2/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p399#2/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p399#2/r1.claim: Qatada explains al-waṣīd as the open space at the cave's entrance.

AKHFASH:v2p429/r1.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v2p429/r1.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v2p429/r1.claim: The singular of أيقاظ is يقظ; the plural of يقظان is يقاظ.

TUSTARI:18:18/r1.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:18:18/r1.speaker: author
TUSTARI:18:18/r1.claim: The dog’s outstretched forelegs signify obedience to command and prohibition.

TUSTARI:18:18/r2.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:18:18/r2.speaker: عكرمة
TUSTARI:18:18/r2.claim: Ikrima says al-raqim means an ink pot in the Roman language.

TUSTARI:18:18/r3.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:18:18/r3.speaker: الحسن
TUSTARI:18:18/r3.claim: Al-Hasan says al-raqim is the valley containing the cave.

TUSTARI:18:18/r4.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:18:18/r4.speaker: كعب
TUSTARI:18:18/r4.claim: Kaʿb says al-raqim is a lead tablet recording the youths’ names, lineages, religion, and origin of flight.

TUSTARI:18:18/r5.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:18:18/r5.speaker: author
TUSTARI:18:18/r5.claim: Al-wasid means the space immediately in front of a door.

TUSTARI:18:18/r6.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:18:18/r6.speaker: author
TUSTARI:18:18/r6.claim: Seeing the youths bodily would make an observer flee, but seeing them through the Real reveals within them the realities of divine unity.

TAB-FULL:v15p170/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p170/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p170/r4.claim: God inspires Deqianus to seal the cave to honor and preserve the youths' bodies until their revival as a sign of resurrection; two secret believers record their names and story on lead tablets in a sealed copper chest.

TAB-FULL:v15p190#3/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p190#3/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p190#3/r1.claim: The sleepers would look awake to an observer; ayqaz is the plural of yaqiz, as illustrated by a rajaz verse, while ruqud is plural of raqid like julus and quʿud.

TAB-FULL:v15p190#3/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p190#3/r2.speaker: الشاعر الراجز
TAB-FULL:v15p190#3/r2.claim: The rajaz poet uses ayqazan as the plural of yaqiz and supports the lexical explanation.

TAB-FULL:v15p190#3/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p190#3/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p190#3/r3.claim: God turns the youths during sleep onto their right sides and then their left sides.

TAB-FULL:v15p190#3/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p190#3/r4.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v15p190#3/r4.claim: Qatada says this turning occurred in their first sleep and reports that Abu Iyad said they were turned twice each year.

TAB-FULL:v15p190#3/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p190#3/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v15p190#3/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas says that without the turning the earth would have eaten them.

TAB-FULL:v15p192/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p192/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p192/r1.claim: Exegetes differ over the dog: some say it was their actual dog, while another account identifies the figure as a human cook who followed them.

TAB-FULL:v15p192/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p192/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p192/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Qatada, and Dahhak gloss wasid as the cave's courtyard or forecourt; Ibn Jurayj says it guards the cave entrance.

TAB-FULL:v15p192/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p192/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v15p192/r3.claim: A separate transmission from Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr says wasid means the ground or open earth.

TAB-FULL:v15p194#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p194#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p194#2/r1.claim: Anyone who looked into the cave would flee in terror because God clothed the sleepers with awe, preventing anyone from reaching or touching them until their appointed awakening.

TAB-FULL:v15p194#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p194#2/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p194#2/r2.claim: Their awakening at God's chosen time makes them a sign that God's promise is true and the Hour is coming without doubt.

TAB-FULL:v15p194#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p194#2/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p194#2/r3.claim: Most Medinan readers use the doubled lam in la-mulliʾta, suggesting repeated filling with terror; Iraqi readers use a light lam, suggesting one filling.

TAB-FULL:v15p194#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p194#2/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p194#2/r4.claim: Both widely transmitted readings are close in meaning and correct.

TAB-FULL:v15p194/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p194/r1.speaker: عمرو
TAB-FULL:v15p194/r1.claim: Amr also explains wasid as the ground or open earth.

TAB-FULL:v15p194/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p194/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v15p194/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses wasid as the door.

TAB-FULL:v15p194/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p194/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p194/r3.claim: He prefers wasid to mean the door or its threshold, where the dog guards the cave, because the word is related to closing a door.

TAB-FULL:v15p194/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p194/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p194/r4.claim: Wasid is the Tihami and Yemeni dialect form alongside Najdi asid, paralleling other dialect pairs with initial waw or hamza.

ZAJJAJ:v3p274/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p274/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p274/r1.claim: Aiqāẓ means awake and ruqūd means asleep; a rajaz poet uses أيقاظا for the awake.

ZAJJAJ:v3p274/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p274/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p274/r2.claim: One interpretation says their eyes were open; the author favors frequent turning as the reason they appear awake, confirmed by the verse.

ZAJJAJ:v3p274/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p274/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p274/r3.claim: The verb تحسبهم is reported with two vocalizations; الوصيد means the house's courtyard.

ZAJJAJ:v3p274/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p274/r4.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p274/r4.claim: Kasra on the wāw in لو اطلعت breaks adjacent sukūns and is more original; ḍamma is also allowed. فرارا is a cognate accusative and رعبا a specification.

ZAJJAJ:v3p274/r5.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p274/r5.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p274/r5.claim: One interpretation says their long hair and nails would frighten anyone who saw them.

NAHHAS:v2p450/r13.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p450/r13.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v2p450/r13.claim: ‘To the right’ and ‘to the left’ are adverbs; ‘in flight’ and ‘with terror’ are accusatives of specification.

NAHHAS:v2p450/r14.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p450/r14.speaker: سيبويه والفراء
NAHHAS:v2p450/r14.claim: They do not allow the specification words ‘in flight’ or ‘with terror’ to precede their governing verbs.

NAHHAS:v2p450/r15.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p450/r15.speaker: محمد بن يزيد
NAHHAS:v2p450/r15.claim: He allows them to precede because the governing verb is inflected.

NAHHAS:v2p450/r16.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p450/r16.speaker: يحيى بن وثاب والأعمش
NAHHAS:v2p450/r16.claim: They read ‘if you looked’ with a damma on the wāw; this is possible because the damma matches it, though kasra is better.

NAHHAS:v2p450/r17.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p450/r17.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v2p450/r17.claim: Firāran is a verbal noun because wallayta here means fararta, ‘you fled.’

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p222/r1.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p222/r1.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p222/r1.claim: The doubled form comes from تَتَزَاوَر with the first tāʾ assimilated into zāy; the light form drops one of two difficult successive tāʾs.

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p222/r2.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p222/r2.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p222/r2.claim: The doubled لام in ولملئت expresses repetition or continuance; the light form indicates a single occurrence.

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p222/r3.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p222/r3.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p222/r3.claim: Hamza in ولملئت follows the original form, while its omission lightens pronunciation; تمليت العيش is always without hamza.

FARISI-HUJJA:v5p134#2/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v5p134#2/r1.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع
FARISI-HUJJA:v5p134#2/r1.claim: They read ولملئت with a doubled lām and hamza; Ibn Kathir also has a reported light form through Ismail b. Muslim.

FARISI-HUJJA:v5p134#2/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v5p134#2/r2.speaker: ابن عامر وعاصم وأبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي
FARISI-HUJJA:v5p134#2/r2.claim: They read ولملئت with a light lām and hamza.

FARISI-HUJJA:v5p134#2/r3.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v5p134#2/r3.speaker: أبو الحسن
FARISI-HUJJA:v5p134#2/r3.claim: Abu al-Hasan considers the light form more idiomatic; examples in poetry and امتلأت support this usage, though a heavy form is also attested in poetry.

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p25/r3.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p25/r3.speaker: الحسن
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p25/r3.claim: Al-Ḥasan reads وتقلبهم as an accusative verbal noun governed by an implied 'We see' or 'We witness,' in keeping with the surrounding observable scenes.

SULAMI:v1p405#2/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p405#2/r1.speaker: ابن عطاء
SULAMI:v1p405#2/r1.claim: They are present in the divine court like sleepers, outside time, place, and worldly access; witnessing consists in stillness under divine attributes.

SULAMI:v1p405#2/r2.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p405#2/r2.speaker: أبو سعيد
SULAMI:v1p405#2/r2.claim: Their state is annihilation and subsistence: they are extinguished through the Real and remain by Him, their own qualities fading as divine qualities appear.

SULAMI:v1p405#2/r3.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p405#2/r3.speaker: أبو سعيد
SULAMI:v1p405#2/r3.claim: As leaders of the unifiers, they saw divine majesty and power, lost pleasure in the created world, and became bewildered between wakefulness and sleep.

SULAMI:v1p406/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p406/r1.speaker: ابن عطاء
SULAMI:v1p406/r1.claim: God turned them through contraction and expansion, gathering and separation, until He gathered them from dispersion into unity.

SULAMI:v1p406/r2.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p406/r2.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v1p406/r2.claim: Their turning means movement among annihilation and subsistence, unveiling and veiling, manifestation and concealment.

SULAMI:v1p406/r3.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p406/r3.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
SULAMI:v1p406/r3.claim: Companionship with the righteous affects a creature's nature; the cave's dog was mentioned with the youths because of its proximity to them.

THALABI:v6p151#2/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p151#2/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p151#2/r2.claim: When the cave opens, God screens the sleepers from people with terror; even the bravest cannot pass the sleeping dog at the entrance.

THALABI:v6p160/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r10.speaker: القرظي
THALABI:v6p160/r10.claim: Al-Qurazi says its strong yellow color tended toward red.

THALABI:v6p160/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r11.speaker: الكلبي
THALABI:v6p160/r11.claim: Al-Kalbi compares the dog's color to khilinj wood.

THALABI:v6p160/r12.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r12.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p160/r12.claim: Other reports compare the dog's color to stone or to the sky.

THALABI:v6p160/r13.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r13.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
THALABI:v6p160/r13.claim: Ali says the dog's name was Rayyan.

THALABI:v6p160/r14.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r14.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v6p160/r14.claim: Ibn Abbas gives the dog the name Qitmir.

THALABI:v6p160/r15.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r15.speaker: الأوزاعي
THALABI:v6p160/r15.claim: Al-Awza'i gives the dog's name as Natwa.

THALABI:v6p160/r16.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r16.speaker: شعيب الجبائي
THALABI:v6p160/r16.claim: Shu'ayb al-Jubba'i gives the dog's name as Hamran.

THALABI:v6p160/r17.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r17.speaker: عبد الله ابن كثير
THALABI:v6p160/r17.claim: Abdullah ibn Kathir gives the dog's name as Qatmur.

THALABI:v6p160/r18.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r18.speaker: السدي
THALABI:v6p160/r18.claim: Al-Suddi gives the dog's name as Nun.

THALABI:v6p160/r19.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r19.speaker: عبد الله بن سلام
THALABI:v6p160/r19.claim: Abdullah ibn Salam gives the dog's name as Basit.

THALABI:v6p160/r20.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r20.speaker: كعب
THALABI:v6p160/r20.claim: Ka'b gives the dog's name as Ashhab.

THALABI:v6p160/r21.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r21.speaker: وهب
THALABI:v6p160/r21.claim: Wahb gives the dog's name as Naqiya, while another report calls it Qutayfir.

THALABI:v6p160/r22.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r22.speaker: عمر
THALABI:v6p160/r22.claim: Umar reports protective invocations associated with a scorpion and a dog, including reciting the cave dog's description when a dog attacks.

THALABI:v6p160/r23.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r23.speaker: جعفر الصادق
THALABI:v6p160/r23.claim: Ja'far al-Sadiq reads kalibahum, meaning the dog's owner or keeper.

THALABI:v6p160/r24.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r24.speaker: مجاهد
THALABI:v6p160/r24.claim: Mujahid and al-Dahhak say al-wasid is the forecourt of the cave; this is also transmitted from Ibn Abbas through Ali ibn Abi Talha.

THALABI:v6p160/r25.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r25.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
THALABI:v6p160/r25.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr interprets al-wasid as the ground or soil, a view transmitted from Ibn Abbas through Atiyya al-Awfi.

THALABI:v6p160/r26.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r26.speaker: السدي
THALABI:v6p160/r26.claim: Al-Suddi says al-wasid means the door, transmitted from Ibn Abbas through Ikrima.

THALABI:v6p160/r27.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r27.speaker: عطاء
THALABI:v6p160/r27.claim: Ata says al-wasid is the threshold of the doorway.

THALABI:v6p160/r28.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r28.speaker: القتيبي
THALABI:v6p160/r28.claim: Al-Qutaybi says al-wasid is the building and relates it to the Arabic verbs for closing a door.

THALABI:v6p160/r29.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r29.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p160/r29.claim: The phrase about turning away means God made the sleepers' appearance prevent anyone from reaching or touching them until the appointed time, when they would become a sign.

THALABI:v6p160/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p160/r3.claim: The youths appear awake though sleeping; yaqaz and ruqud are plural forms for alert and sleeping people, respectively.

THALABI:v6p160/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r4.speaker: الحسن
THALABI:v6p160/r4.claim: Al-Hasan reads the verb for turning them with a lightened consonant.

THALABI:v6p160/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v6p160/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas says they were turned onto a different side once each year to keep the ground from consuming their flesh.

THALABI:v6p160/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r6.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p160/r6.claim: One report says their turning took place on Ashura.

THALABI:v6p160/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r7.speaker: أبو هريرة
THALABI:v6p160/r7.claim: Abu Hurayra says they were turned twice each year.

THALABI:v6p160/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v6p160/r8.claim: Ibn Abbas describes the dog as brindled.

THALABI:v6p160/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p160/r9.speaker: مقاتل
THALABI:v6p160/r9.claim: Muqatil says the dog was yellow.

THALABI:v6p161/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p161/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p161/r1.claim: Rعب means fear; Medina readers use a doubled form for 'you would be filled,' and explanations include the place's eerie look, open eyes, or God's protective terror.

THALABI:v6p161/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p161/r2.speaker: الكلبي
THALABI:v6p161/r2.claim: Al-Kalbi says the youths' open eyes make them look like sleepers about to speak, causing terror.

THALABI:v6p161/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p161/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p161/r3.claim: Another view says God protected the youths from being seen by frightening people away.

THALABI:v6p161/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p161/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v6p161/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas tells that on a Roman campaign Muawiya wanted to uncover the cave, but Ibn Abbas said God had barred someone better than Muawiya from seeing them.

THALABI:v6p161/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p161/r5.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p161/r5.claim: When Muawiya sent men to inspect the cave, a wind drove them out and terror prevented them from seeing the youths.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r1.claim: They appear awake while sleeping; awake means alert and sleeping means asleep, and one report says their eyes remained open and they breathed without speaking.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r11.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r11.speaker: اليزيدي
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r11.claim: الوصيد may mean an enclosure or pen.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r12.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r12.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r12.claim: الوصيد may mean soil, by association with الصعيد.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r13.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r13.speaker: عطية
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r13.claim: الوصيد may mean a door; a poet's line uses the word in the phrase لا يسد وصيدها.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r14.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r14.speaker: جرير بن عبيد
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r14.claim: Jarir ibn Ubayd reports that the dog was a small pet kept nearby.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r15.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r15.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r15.claim: Ibn Ishaq says the dog was yellow.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r16.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r16.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r16.claim: A visitor would flee in fear because the youths' long nails and hair were frightening.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r17.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r17.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r17.claim: Alternatively, God clothed them in awe that turned people's eyes away until their appointed term, keeping intruders from them.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r18.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r18.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r18.claim: Ibn Abbas says that during a Roman naval campaign with Muawiya, Muawiya wanted to enter the cave; Ibn Abbas said God had prevented someone better than him. A party sent inside was driven out by a wind.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r19.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r19.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r19.claim: An alternative account says this sign occurred before their people for a prophet said to have been one of the youths, the leader they followed and believed.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r2.claim: They were turned from side to side as sleepers are, so the earth would not consume their bodies during their long stay.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says they were turned twice each year, six months on each side.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r4.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r4.claim: Mujahid says they were turned only during the first nine years, not during the following three hundred.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r5.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r5.claim: Their appearance of wakefulness may be due to their open eyes.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r6.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r6.claim: Alternatively, their turning from side to side made them look awake.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r7.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r7.claim: The dog was an actual dog, as the majority say; another account calls it Himran.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r8.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r8.claim: Alternatively, it was a human cook who followed the youths, or a shepherd.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r9.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p291#2/r9.claim: الوصيد may mean a threshold or doorstep.

QUSHAYRI:v2p212/r3.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p212/r3.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p212/r3.claim: The youths were outwardly present to observers but inwardly absorbed and effaced in what was unveiled to them of the Real; in reality another acted through them.

QUSHAYRI:v2p212/r4.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p212/r4.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p212/r4.claim: Turning them from side to side describes God's sheltering care, more complete than a mother's tenderness and more precious than a father's mercy.

QUSHAYRI:v2p212/r5.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p212/r5.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p212/r5.claim: The knowers of unity appear outwardly differentiated but inwardly witness unity, and their actions unfold without affectation.

QUSHAYRI:v2p212/r6.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p212/r6.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p212/r6.claim: A lover loves those associated with the beloved; the dog is remembered alongside the youths through the Resurrection.

QUSHAYRI:v2p212/r7.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p212/r7.speaker: التفاسير
QUSHAYRI:v2p212/r7.claim: A reported version says the shepherd would not send away the dog because he had raised it; another says God made the dog speak and refuse to leave its caretaker.

QUSHAYRI:v2p212/r8.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p212/r8.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p212/r8.claim: The dog's lowly value and impure qualities did not harm it because it kept company with the youths.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r1.claim: The address is hypothetical like the earlier mention of seeing the sun: if one saw them, one would think they were awake.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r2.speaker: الأخفش وأبو عبيدة والزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r2.claim: They give ayqāẓ as a plural form of ayqaẓ, yaqīẓ, and yaqẓān; Ruʾba verse uses the word.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r3.claim: Ruqud means sleepers and is a verbal noun used collectively like bowing, sitting, and prostrating; calling it a plural of raqid is morphologically remote.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r4.speaker: الكلبي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r4.claim: He says they seemed awake because their eyes were open.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r5.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r5.claim: He explains their appearance as awake by their frequent turning from side to side, supported by the following statement that God turned them.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r6.speaker: أبو عياض
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r6.claim: Qatada transmits that Abu Iyad said they were turned over twice each year; Abu Hurayra is also said to hold this view.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r7.claim: He says the turning prevented the earth from consuming their flesh and wearing their bodies away.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r8.speaker: مجاهد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r8.claim: In a report through Ibn Abi Najih, they slept on their right sides for nine years, then on their left for nine years.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r9.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p556/r9.claim: Dhāt is an adverb meaning on the side of the right, as in the earlier phrase about the sun direction.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p558/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p558/r1.speaker: ابن عباس وأكثر المفسرين
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p558/r1.claim: They say the youths fled their king by night, met a shepherd with a dog, and the shepherd followed them in faith with his dog.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p558/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p558/r2.speaker: كعب
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p558/r2.claim: He tells that the dog barked, was repeatedly driven off, then spoke of loving God beloved and offered to guard the youths while they slept.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p558/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p558/r3.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p558/r3.claim: He says the dog was used for hunting.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p558/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p558/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p558/r4.claim: The dog stretched both arms flat on the ground rather than drawing them inward; a Prophetic report prohibits spreading the forearms in prayer like a beast.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p558/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p558/r5.speaker: الحديث
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p558/r5.claim: A Prophetic report forbids laying the forearms flat in prayer like a wild animal.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p558/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p558/r6.speaker: الليث
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p558/r6.claim: He defines the forearm as extending from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger; Ibn al-Sikkit says the noun is feminine.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p558/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p558/r7.speaker: أبو علي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p558/r7.claim: The active participle basit governs its object because the scene is presented as ongoing; if the action were simply past, it would lose the participle verbal force.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r1.claim: In reports through Ali and Ata, he glosses waṣīd as the forecourt; Mujahid and al-Dahhak, most exegetes, and most lexicographers agree.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r10.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r10.claim: Both door and courtyard readings work: a sealed cave entrance makes the dog at the door, while the area outside the cave mouth is its forecourt; Saʿid ibn Jubayr ground or dust likely means forecourt.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r2.speaker: أبو عبيد عن الأحمر
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r2.claim: Al-Ahmar glosses waṣīd as a courtyard or open space.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r3.speaker: الزجاج وأبو عبيدة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r3.claim: Al-Zajjaj calls it the house or home forecourt; Abu Ubayda gives plural forms wasaʾid and waṣd.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r4.speaker: يونس والأخفش والفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r4.claim: They treat waṣīd and aṣīd as dialect variants, like wakāf and ikāf.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r5.speaker: الكسائي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r5.claim: He assigns waṣīd to Tihama and aṣīd to Najd, and says the Quran was revealed in Tihama speech.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r6.speaker: السدي عن عكرمة عن ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r6.claim: This report interprets waṣīd as the door.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r7.speaker: المبرد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r7.claim: He prefers door: being at the door means being in its vicinity.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r8.speaker: عطاء وابن قتيبة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r8.claim: Ata says threshold, and Ibn Qutayba prefers that sense because a closed door meets the threshold; the cave had no literal threshold, so the dog occupied its place, though waṣīd may also mean door.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r9.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p560/r9.claim: The derivation from asada and awsada, to shut a door, supports door or sealed entrance; readings of the closed-door term correspond to aṣīd or waṣīd.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p563/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p563/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p563/r1.claim: Ittalaʿa means to look over or appear above something, as in the verse about the speaker looking down and seeing his companion.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p563/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p563/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p563/r2.claim: Lawallayta means turn away and flee; firāran is accusative as a verbal noun because the verb sense is fleeing.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p563/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p563/r3.speaker: المفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p563/r3.claim: God filled a viewer with fear to prevent anyone from seeing the youths.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p563/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p563/r4.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p563/r4.claim: Another explanation says their very long hair and fingernails would frighten anyone who saw them.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p563/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p563/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p563/r5.claim: The light reading of l-muliʾta is preferred because Arabs commonly say fear filled me, while the heavy form is little known; poems attest both forms.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:17-18/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:17-18/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:17-18/r3.claim: Their eyes were open, so they appeared awake while sleeping; God turned them from side to side to keep the ground from consuming their flesh.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:17-18/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:17-18/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:17-18/r4.claim: The dog stretched its forelegs at the cave entrance; anyone seeing the youths would flee in terror because God used fear to keep people away.

JISHUMI:v6p4371/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4371/r2.speaker: أبو جعفر ونافع وابن كثير
JISHUMI:v6p4371/r2.claim: They read ولملئت with doubled lām and hamza; the others lighten it, with one report from Ibn Kathīr also light, and doubling adds emphasis.

JISHUMI:v6p4371/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4371/r3.speaker: أبو جعفر وابن عامر والكسائي ويعقوب
JISHUMI:v6p4371/r3.claim: They read رعب with ḍamma on ʿayn throughout the Qurʾān; the others use sukūn, as two dialects.

JISHUMI:v6p4371/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4371/r5.speaker: الحسن
JISHUMI:v6p4371/r5.claim: He reads نقلبهم without doubling; the common doubled form adds emphasis.

JISHUMI:v6p4371/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4371/r6.speaker: الصادق
JISHUMI:v6p4371/r6.claim: A report from al-Ṣādiq reads كالبهم, meaning the dog's owner, but the author says recitation must follow the widespread, continuously transmitted reading.

JISHUMI:v6p4373/r16.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4373/r16.speaker: أبو علي وجماعة
JISHUMI:v6p4373/r16.claim: They say the youths appeared awake although asleep because their eyes were open and they breathed but did not speak.

JISHUMI:v6p4376/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r1.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r1.claim: God turned them from side to side so ground moisture would not harm them and they would not suffer from lying on one side.

JISHUMI:v6p4376/r10.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r10.speaker: عطاء
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r10.claim: He explains waṣīd as the threshold of the door.

JISHUMI:v6p4376/r11.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r11.speaker: القتبي
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r11.claim: He explains waṣīd as a building.

JISHUMI:v6p4376/r12.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r12.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r12.claim: If a person saw them in the cave, he would flee from them and be filled with fear; another report says God clothed them in awe.

JISHUMI:v6p4376/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r2.claim: He says they were turned once a year so the earth would not consume their flesh.

JISHUMI:v6p4376/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r3.speaker: قيل
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r3.claim: One account says their turning occurred on ʿĀshūrāʾ.

JISHUMI:v6p4376/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r4.speaker: أبو هريرة
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r4.claim: He says they were turned twice each year.

JISHUMI:v6p4376/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r5.speaker: قيل
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r5.claim: Reports differ on the dog: it was theirs, a shepherd's, or their cook's; Ibn ʿAbbās calls it dark brown and Muqātil calls it yellow.

JISHUMI:v6p4376/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r6.speaker: أبو علي
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r6.claim: One report gives the dog the name Rayyān.

JISHUMI:v6p4376/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r7.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة والضحاك والأصم
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r7.claim: They are reported to call the dog Qiṭmīr.

JISHUMI:v6p4376/r8.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r8.claim: He explains waṣīd as the doorway; Abū ʿAlī places the dog at the opening of the broad chamber.

JISHUMI:v6p4376/r9.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r9.speaker: سعيد بن جبير وعطية عن ابن عباس
JISHUMI:v6p4376/r9.claim: They explain waṣīd as the ground or soil.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r10.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r10.speaker: القرظي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r10.claim: He describes an intense yellow color tending toward red.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r11.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r11.speaker: الكلبي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r11.claim: He compares its color to khalanj wood; another view says it was stone-colored.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r14.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r14.speaker: الأوزاعي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r14.claim: He gives the dog's name as Batur; al-Suddī calls it Tūr and Kaʿb calls it Ṣuhayla.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r15.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r15.speaker: خالد بن معدان
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r15.claim: He says the only animals in Paradise are the Companions of the Cave's dog and Balaam's donkey.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r2.claim: They appeared awake because their eyes were open and they breathed, though they did not speak.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r3.claim: He says they were turned from one side to another once a year so the earth would not consume their flesh.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r4.claim: Other reports say they were turned on ʿĀshūrāʾ or twice each year.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r5.speaker: أكثر أهل التفسير
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r5.claim: Most exegetes say the animal with its forelegs outstretched at the entrance was a dog.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r6.speaker: ابن جريج
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r6.claim: He says it was a lion called a dog, citing the Prophet's supplication against ʿUtba ibn Abī Lahab, after which a lion devoured him.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r7.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r7.claim: Baghawī judges the ordinary dog interpretation more sound.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r8.claim: He describes the dog as white-marked; another report puts it above the qalṭī dog and below the Kurdish dog, glossing qalṭī as Chinese.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r9.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r9.speaker: مقاتل
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p157#2/r9.claim: He says the dog was yellow.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p158/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p158/r1.speaker: مجاهد والضحاك
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p158/r1.claim: They interpret waṣīd as the courtyard of the cave.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p158/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p158/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p158/r2.claim: Baghawī reports ʿAṭāʾ's interpretation of waṣīd as the threshold; he clarifies that the term can mean the place of a door or threshold even when the cave has none.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p158/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p158/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p158/r3.claim: Baghawī reports al-Suddī's interpretation of waṣīd as a door, also transmitted by ʿIkrima from Ibn Abbas.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p158/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p158/r4.speaker: السدي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p158/r4.claim: He says the dog turned with the sleepers, folding the ear against whichever side it lay on.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p158/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p158/r5.speaker: أهل الحجاز
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p158/r5.claim: The Hijazi readers double the lām in lamilta; other readers lighten it.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p158/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p158/r6.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p158/r6.claim: The terror is variously attributed to the cave's desolation, open eyes, abundant hair and long nails with movement, or God's preventing people from approaching.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p158/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p158/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p158/r7.claim: On campaign with Muʿāwiya toward Byzantine lands, Ibn Abbas objected when Muʿāwiya proposed uncovering the sleepers; God sent a wind that drove the men from the cave.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r1.claim: Taḥsabuhum is read with either vowel on the sīn and addresses any observer; yaqiz means awake. Their open eyes, frequent turning, or turning once or twice yearly may make them appear awake.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r10.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r10.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r10.claim: A reading of law iṭṭalaʿta has ḍamma on the wāw.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r2.claim: The sleepers are read as being turned by God, or their turning is read as a verbal noun governed by an implied verb.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r3.claim: Another reading has kālibuhum, meaning the companion of their dog, rather than their dog.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r4.claim: Bāsiṭ dhirāʿayhi depicts a past scene; the active participle's annexation is genuinely definite only if the past is narrated as present.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r5.claim: Al-Waṣīd means the courtyard, threshold, or door; a cited poem witnesses its use for a threshold.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r6.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r6.claim: Li-muliʾat is read with a doubled lām for emphasis; the hamza may be eased and changed to yāʾ, and ruʿban is read light or heavy.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r7.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r7.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r7.claim: Their terrifying appearance may come from divine awe, long nails and hair and huge bodies, or the desolation of the place.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r8.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r8.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r8.claim: During a Roman campaign, Muʿāwiya wanted to view the sleepers; Ibn ʿAbbās said God had barred someone better than him, but Muʿāwiya sent men who were burned by a wind in the cave.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r9.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p662/r9.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās told Muʿāwiya that he had no right to uncover the sleepers, since God had prevented someone better than him from doing so.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p503/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p503/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p503/r6.claim: The verse narrates a past condition with present-tense verbs for vividness; ayqaz is the plural of yaqiz, an awake person.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p503/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p503/r7.speaker: أهل التفسير
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p503/r7.claim: Commentators say their eyes were open while they slept, making an observer think they were awake.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p503/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p503/r8.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p503/r8.claim: The author also suggests they seemed alert because they were carefully preserved and had not acquired the usual relaxed appearance of sleepers; open eyes would make this still clearer if reliably transmitted.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504#2/r1.speaker: المهدوي والزجاج
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504#2/r1.claim: Al-Mahdawi and al-Zajjaj suggest their frightening hair and nails caused the terror, but the author calls this far-fetched.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504#2/r2.claim: God preserved their sleeping appearance as a sign: their clothes and bodies did not change, while the awakened youth noticed only changes to the land and buildings.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504#2/r3.speaker: أبو حاتم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504#2/r3.claim: Abu Hatim says both pronunciations of ruʿban, with a silent or rounded ʿayn, are valid dialect forms.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r1.claim: The author argues that the verse presents the turning as a separate report, not as the reason observers thought the youths were awake.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r10.speaker: أبو الفضل الجوهري
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r10.claim: A preacher, as heard by Ibn Atiyya's father, said that loving virtuous people brings blessing, citing the dog remembered in the Qur'an because it accompanied good people.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r11.speaker: الطبري
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r11.claim: Al-Tabari reports unnamed views that the dog was a cook among the youths or one of the youths stationed as a lookout; the author says the human reading is weakened by the extended arms, a dog's familiar posture.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r12.speaker: أبو عمر المطرز
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r12.claim: Abu Umar al-Muṭarriz reports a reading kalibahum, which may mean a human sentry lying low with arms extended or the dog itself.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r13.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r13.claim: The active participle bāsit is used with past meaning because the verse depicts a scene; wasid means the cave threshold or its site, with courtyard, door, and ground also reported, and the author prefers threshold.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r14.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r14.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وابن جبير
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r14.claim: They gloss wasid as a courtyard; Ibn Abbas also says door and Ibn Jubayr also says earth.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r15.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r15.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r15.claim: Most readers pronounce law iṭṭalaʿta with kasra on wāw, while some use ḍamma; the lam in lamilʾta is geminated by one group to intensify the sense, but plain form is more common.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r16.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r16.speaker: المخبل السعدي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r16.claim: Al-Mukhabbal al-Saʿdi's verse attests the intensified form of the verb meaning to be filled.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r2.claim: The author reports al-Hasan's alternate reading of the turning phrase, prefers Abu Hatim's syntax over Ibn Jinni's, and treats the turning as a separate reported action.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r3.speaker: أبو عياض
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r3.claim: Abu Iyad says the sleepers were turned over twice a year.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r4.speaker: فرقة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r4.claim: One group says they were turned once every seven years.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r5.speaker: فرقة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r5.claim: Another group restricts the turning to the final nine years.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas says the turning protected them from the ground, and sunlight would have burned them; without turning, earth would have consumed them.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r7.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r7.claim: The author says avoiding feeding, sunlight, and contact with the ground through such a long sleep is more wondrous than simply preserving them from sun and earth; the reports are conjectural.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r8.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r8.claim: Commentators generally attribute the turning to God's command and the angels; the author allows instead that God enabled the living youths to turn without waking.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r9.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p504/r9.claim: Most commentators say the dog was real and belonged to a hunter among them; another account has a shepherd and his dog join the youths.

TABRISI:18:17-18#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18#2/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:18:17-18#2/r3.claim: The active participle bāsiṭ governs ‘his forelegs’ despite referring to the past, because the narrative depicts the scene as present.

TABRISI:18:17-18#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18#2/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:18:17-18#2/r5.claim: The wāw in iṭṭalaʿtum may have kasra, which is preferred between two vowelless consonants, or ḍamma by assimilation to wāw; ḍamma is favored when the next syllable is also ḍamma.

TABRISI:18:17-18#2/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18#2/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:18:17-18#2/r6.claim: Firāran is a verbal noun because wallayta means ‘you fled’; raʿban is a specification, as in ‘filled with fear’ or ‘the vessel filled with water.’

TABRISI:18:17-18#3/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18#3/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:18:17-18#3/r10.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that they were turned once each year.

TABRISI:18:17-18#3/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18#3/r11.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:18:17-18#3/r11.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and most commentators say the youths fled their ruler by night, met a shepherd with a dog, and the dog followed them in their faith.

TABRISI:18:17-18#3/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18#3/r6.speaker: الجبائي
TABRISI:18:17-18#3/r6.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī and others say the youths appeared awake because their eyes were open and they breathed as though about to speak, though they did not.

TABRISI:18:17-18#3/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18#3/r7.speaker: قيل
TABRISI:18:17-18#3/r7.claim: Alternatively, they turned over just as awake people do.

TABRISI:18:17-18#3/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18#3/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:18:17-18#3/r8.claim: God turned them periodically from one side to the other so the earth would not consume them and their clothes would not decay from lying on one side.

TABRISI:18:17-18#3/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18#3/r9.speaker: أبو هريرة
TABRISI:18:17-18#3/r9.claim: Abū Hurayra reports that they were turned twice each year.

TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r1.speaker: كعب
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r1.claim: Kaʿb gives another account: after repeatedly driving the dog away, the youths heard it say it loved God’s friends and would guard them, then it slept beside them.

TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r10.speaker: قيل
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r10.claim: Alternatively, the eerie setting terrified people who came to the cave, and unbelievers sealed its entrance to kill the youths; God made this a protection for them.

TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r11.speaker: author
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r11.claim: The suggestion that long nails and hair caused the terror is unsound, since the youths later said they had slept only a day or part of one.

TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r12.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r12.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r12.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr reports Ibn ʿAbbās telling Muʿāwiya during a Roman campaign that no one, even someone better than him, was permitted to uncover the youths; when Muʿāwiya sent men into the cave, God sent wind that drove them out.

TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r2.speaker: مقاتل
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r2.claim: Muqātil says the dog was yellow.

TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r3.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the dog was spotted and named Qiṭmīr.

TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r4.speaker: الحسن
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r4.claim: Al-Ḥasan’s commentary says the dog remained there for 309 years without food, drink, sleep, or rising.

TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r5.claim: Bāsiṭ dhirāʿayh means laying both forelegs flat on the ground, like a lion lying down.

TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r6.claim: Waṣīd means the cave’s courtyard according to Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Qatāda; others say the entrance, the recess entrance, or the threshold.

TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r7.speaker: الجبائي
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r7.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī places the dog by the entrance of the recess, not the cave entrance, reasoning that searchers would otherwise have entered or found it; shepherds later moved the stones and used the opening as a livestock enclosure.

TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r8.speaker: عطاء
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r8.claim: ʿAṭāʾ says waṣīd is the door’s threshold.

TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:18:17-18#4/r9.claim: Anyone who looked into the cave would flee in terror; God kept people away until the appointed time and protected the sleepers from predators and other harm.

TABRISI:18:17-18/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18/r5.speaker: أبو الحسن
TABRISI:18:17-18/r5.claim: Abū al-Ḥasan considers the lighter lummilt more idiomatic, since people usually say ‘you filled me with fear’ rather than ‘fear filled me.’

TABRISI:18:17-18/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:18:17-18/r6.claim: Poetry by Imruʾ al-Qays and al-Aʿshā supports the lighter form, while al-Mukhabbal al-Saʿdī supplies an example of the intensified form.

TABRISI:18:17-18/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:17-18/r7.speaker: الحسن
TABRISI:18:17-18/r7.claim: Al-Ḥasan’s variant reads ‘and their turning’ as an active verb, with an understood verb such as ‘you see’ governing it.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r1.speaker: الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r1.claim: A person who is alert is called يقظ or يقظان; the plural is أيقاظ, while رقود means sleepers.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r10.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r10.speaker: ابن عباس عن ابن أبي طلحة وسعيد بن جبير ومجاهد والضحاك وقتادة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r10.claim: One view makes الوصيد the cave's courtyard; the words الوصيد and الأصيد are dialectal variants, also meaning enclosure or courtyard.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r11.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r11.speaker: الفراء
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r11.claim: The Hijaz says الوصيد, while Najd says الأصيد; both are dialectal words for an enclosure or courtyard.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r12.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r12.speaker: عكرمة عن ابن عباس والسدي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r12.claim: A second view identifies الوصيد as the door; Ibn Qutayba understands the dog to lie at the door and cites a poem.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r13.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r13.speaker: العوفي عن ابن عباس وسعيد بن جبير ومجاهد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r13.claim: A third view takes الوصيد to mean the ground or open earth.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r14.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r14.speaker: عطاء
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r14.claim: A fourth view understands الوصيد as the door threshold.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r15.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r15.speaker: ابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r15.claim: He prefers threshold: the root describes closing a door against its sill, and this permits the dog to be at the cave entrance whether inside or outside.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r2.speaker: الفراء
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r2.claim: The singular of أيقاظ is يقظ; he also gives يقظ as its singular form.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r3.speaker: ابن السائب
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r3.claim: They look awake because their eyes are open while they sleep.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r4.speaker: بعض أهل العلم
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r4.claim: Another explanation is that their eyes remain open because they would melt if kept closed continuously.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r5.speaker: أبو رجاء
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r5.claim: He reads the verb with feminine tāʾ and a light lām, describing them as being turned.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r6.speaker: أبو الجوزاء وعكرمة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r6.claim: They use the same reading with nūn instead of tāʾ.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r7.claim: They were turned twice each year, spending six months on each side so the earth would not consume their flesh.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r8.speaker: مجاهد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r8.claim: They lay on one side for three hundred years, then were turned for the remaining nine.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r9.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p118#2/r9.claim: The dog shared their sleeping state but appeared alert to the eye.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r1.claim: As with “you see the sun,” the wording means that if one saw the sleepers one would think they were awake.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r10.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r10.claim: Rāzī rejects these precise schedules: reason cannot determine them, the Qurʾān does not specify them, and no sound report establishes them.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r11.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r11.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r11.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says turning them prevented the earth from eating their flesh or wearing them away.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r12.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r12.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r12.claim: Rāzī finds that rationale strange: the God who kept them alive for over three hundred years could preserve their bodies without turning them.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r13.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r13.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r13.claim: Dhāt is adverbial here, meaning on the side or in the direction of the right or left, as in the previous verse.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r14.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r14.speaker: ابن عباس وأكثر المفسرين
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r14.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and most commentators say the youths fled by night and a shepherd's dog followed them in their faith.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r15.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r15.speaker: كعب
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r15.claim: Kaʿb says a dog repeatedly barked after them; it then declared love for God's beloved and offered to guard them.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r16.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r16.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r16.claim: ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr says the dog was their hunting dog.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r17.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r17.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r17.claim: The dog's outstretched forelegs lay flat on the ground, like the posture the Prophet prohibited in prayer when he likened it to a lion's sprawl.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r18.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r18.speaker: الزجاج
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r18.claim: Al-Zajjāj says waṣīd is the forecourt or entrance of a house or dwelling and gives its plurals.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r19.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r19.speaker: يونس والأخفش والفراء
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r19.claim: Yūnus, al-Akhfash, and al-Farrāʾ treat waṣīd and aṣīd as dialect variants, like wakāf and ikāf.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r2.speaker: الأخفش وأبو عبيدة والزجاج
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r2.claim: Al-Akhfash, Abū ʿUbayda, and al-Zajjāj say ayqāẓ is the plural of yaqiz or yaqẓān; a verse by Ruʾba illustrates the word.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r20.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r20.speaker: السدي
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r20.claim: Al-Suddī says waṣīd means the door; the cave had no actual door or threshold, so the dog occupied the threshold's position.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r21.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r21.speaker: الزجاج
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r21.claim: Al-Zajjāj explains iṭṭalaʿta ʿalayhim as looking down on them or seeing them from above.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r22.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r22.speaker: الزجاج
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r22.claim: Al-Zajjāj says farāran is a cognate accusative because wallayta means “you fled.”

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r23.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r23.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r23.claim: Some explain the terror by their long hair and nails and open eyes while asleep; another view says God made anyone who saw them panic, which Rāzī considers sounder while leaving the precise cause to God.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r24.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r24.speaker: نافع وابن كثير
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r24.claim: Nāfiʿ and Ibn Kathīr read lamuʾiʾt with a doubled lām; the rest lighten it, and one transmission from Ibn Kathīr also lightens it. The senses are alike, with doubling more emphatic.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r25.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r25.speaker: الأخفش
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r25.claim: Al-Akhfash says the light reading is more idiomatic Arabic; poetic usage supports it, though the doubled form is also attested.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r3.speaker: رؤبة
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r3.claim: Ruʾba's line uses ayqāẓ for awake people: “they found their brothers awake.”

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r4.claim: Ruqūd means sleeping; it is a verbal noun used adjectivally for a plural, and Rāzī rejects deriving it as the plural of rāqid because that pattern is unattested for active participles.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r5.speaker: الواحدي
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r5.claim: Al-Wāḥidī says their open eyes made them appear awake.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r6.speaker: الزجاج
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r6.claim: Al-Zajjāj says their repeated turning made them look awake, as the following clause explains.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r7.speaker: أبو هريرة
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r7.claim: A report from Abū Hurayra says they were turned onto their sides twice each year.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r8.speaker: مجاهد
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r8.claim: Mujāhid says they remained on their right sides for nine years, then on their left sides for nine years.

RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p85#3/r9.claim: Another report says they were turned only once, on the day of ʿĀshūrāʾ.

RAZI-FULL:v21p86/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p86/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p86/r1.claim: Several poetic lines attest the light reading of “filled me with terror,” while a line by al-Mukhabbal al-Saʿdī attests the doubled form.

RAZI-FULL:v21p86/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p86/r2.speaker: ابن عامر والكسائي
RAZI-FULL:v21p86/r2.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir and al-Kisāʾī pronounce the ʿayn of ruʿban with ḍamma throughout the Qurʾān; the other readers use sukūn.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r1.speaker: أهل التفسير
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r1.claim: They seemed awake because their eyes were open; another view says their frequent turning made them look awake.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r10.speaker: علي
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r10.claim: Ali names the dog Rayyan; Ibn Abbas calls it Qitmir, al-Awzaʿi Mushir, Ibn Salam Basit, Kaʿb Suhya, Wahb Naqiya, and another report Qutayfur.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r11.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r11.claim: Keeping a dog was permitted in their time, as hunting, herding, and crop dogs are permitted under Islamic law.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r12.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r12.claim: Ibn Abbas says seven youths fled by night and joined a shepherd who had a dog; the shepherd adopted their faith.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r13.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r13.speaker: كعب
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r13.claim: Kaʿb says the dog returned after being chased away, raised its paws in prayer, spoke of loving God's beloved, and promised to guard them.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r2.claim: Ruqud is a collective description by a verbal noun, like saying a people are bowing, prostrating, or sitting.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says God turned them from side to side so the earth would not consume their flesh.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r4.speaker: أبو هريرة
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r4.claim: Abu Hurayra says they were turned twice each year; another report says once a year.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r5.speaker: مجاهد
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r5.claim: Mujahid says they were turned once every seven years.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r6.speaker: فرقة
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r6.claim: One group says they were turned only during the final nine years, not throughout the first three hundred.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r7.claim: Commentators generally attribute the turning to God, but it could have been performed by an angel at God's command.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r8.speaker: عمرو بن دينار
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r8.claim: A saying attributed to Amr ibn Dinar claims a scorpion does not harm someone who blesses Noah, and a dog will not harm someone reciting the cave-dog clause.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r9.speaker: مقاتل
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#2/r9.claim: Most commentators take the dog as a literal dog kept for hunting, crops, or sheep; its color traditions conflict, listing nearly every possible color.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r1.speaker: النبي ﷺ
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r1.claim: The sound report from Ibn Umar says keeping a dog outside hunting or herding reduces one's reward by two qirats daily.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r2.speaker: النبي ﷺ
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r2.claim: A sound report from Abu Hurayra includes crop dogs among the exceptions and states a one-qirat daily loss otherwise.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r3.speaker: الزهري
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r3.claim: When told Abu Hurayra's version, Ibn Umar was excused by al-Zuhri as a farmer who kept a crop dog.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r4.claim: Proposed reasons for the reward loss include frightening Muslims, disturbance by barking, angels' exclusion, impurity according to al-Shafiʿi, or keeping an animal without benefit.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r5.claim: The one- and two-qirat versions may distinguish more harmful dogs, such as the black dog called a devil, or vary by location; permitted working dogs incur no loss.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r6.speaker: النبي ﷺ
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r6.claim: A Jabir report calls a black dog with two spots a devil, in the context of the command to kill black dogs.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r7.speaker: مالك
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r7.claim: Malik permits a sheep dog that accompanies the flock and a crop dog that guards crops from wild animals, but not one used to guard a home from thieves.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#3/r8.claim: Other jurists also permit dogs guarding livestock or crops against thieves.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r1.claim: The dog's companionship consoles imperfect believers who love the Prophet, his family, and the righteous: if a dog is remembered with its beloved group, believers may hope for mercy.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r10.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وابن جبير
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r10.claim: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Ibn Jubayr gloss al-wasid as the cave courtyard; Ibn Abbas also says it means the door, and Ata says the threshold.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r2.speaker: النبي ﷺ
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r2.claim: When a man said he had little prayer, fasting, or charity but loved God and the Messenger, the Prophet told him he would be with those he loved.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r3.speaker: أنس بن مالك
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r3.claim: Anas says no joy after Islam surpassed hearing that he would be with those he loved; he loved God, the Prophet, Abu Bakr, and Umar and hoped to join them.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r4.speaker: فرقة
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r4.claim: A group says the 'dog' was a human lookout stationed by the cave, named by analogy to a companion star of Gemini or Orion.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r5.speaker: ابن عطية
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r5.claim: Ibn Atiyya says the human-guard reading is weakened by the description of outstretched forelegs, an ordinary canine posture.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r6.speaker: أبو عمر المطرز
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r6.claim: Abu Umar al-Mutarriz records a reading kalibihim that could mean their human keeper or their dog.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r7.speaker: جعفر بن محمد الصادق
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r7.claim: Jaʿfar al-Sadiq reads the phrase as their keeper, kalibihim.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r8.claim: Basit is an active participle used with past reference because the verse narrates a scene rather than reporting the dog's action as a new event; a forearm runs from elbow to middle finger.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#4/r9.claim: The dog may have stretched its forelegs because of the long duration, or it may have been asleep, perhaps with open eyes as a sign.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r1.claim: An unnamed poem uses waṣīd for an entryway; the word can also mean a closed door or closely growing plants.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r2.claim: Anyone who looked toward them would flee from divinely imposed terror; some attribute the reaction to the cave's eerie location or a barrier of fear around them.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r3.speaker: المهدوي والنحاس والزجاج والقشيري
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r3.claim: They suggest that the youths' long hair and nails caused the terror; al-Qurtubi calls this unlikely because they thought they had slept only a day.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r4.speaker: ابن عطية
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r4.claim: Ibn Atiyya says God preserved their sleeping appearance and clothing as a sign; only the landscape and buildings changed, so hair and nails were not altered.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r5.speaker: نافع وابن كثير وابن عباس وأهل مكة والمدينة
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r5.claim: They read lammuliʾta with a doubled lām for emphatic intensification; the other readers use the lighter, more common form.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r6.speaker: المخبل السعدي
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r6.claim: Al-Mukhabbal al-Saʿdi's line supplies a poetic example of the doubled form.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r7.speaker: أبو جعفر
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r7.claim: Abu Jaʿfar reads ruʿban with ḍamma on ʿayn; Abu Hatim says both vowelings are Arabic dialects.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:17-18#5/r8.claim: Fararan is a circumstantial accusative; ruʿban is either a second object or a specification accusative.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:18/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:18/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:18/r1.claim: They seem awake because their eyes are open or they turn frequently, although they sleep; God turns them to keep the ground from consuming the sides touching it.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:18/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:18/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:18/r2.claim: The action is also read with a yāʾ and God as subject, or as the verbal noun describing their turning.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:18/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:18/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:18/r3.claim: The dog may have been a stray that followed and was divinely made to speak, or a shepherd's dog; the reading كالبهم supports an owner of a dog.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:18/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:18/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:18/r4.claim: The participle basit depicts the dog's past state, while waṣīd means the cave's yard, entrance, or threshold.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:18/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:18/r5.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:18/r5.claim: An observer would flee in terror because divine awe enveloped the sleepers, their bodies were imposing and eyes open, or the place was desolate.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:18/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:18/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:18/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas warned Muawiya that God had barred even a better man from looking at the sleepers; Muawiya sent men anyway, and a wind burned them.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:18/r7.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:18/r7.speaker: الحجازيان
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:18/r7.claim: The Hijazi readers double the consonant in لملئت for emphasis; Ibn Amir, al-Kisa'i, and Yaqub read رعبا with a heavy consonant.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r1.claim: The verse's recitation of taḥsabuhum with fatḥa on the sīn is attributed to the Syrian readers.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r2.claim: They seem awake because their eyes are open while they are actually asleep.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r3.claim: One report says they were turned twice each year; another says once on the day of ʿĀshūrāʾ.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r4.claim: The dog is described with an active participle for a past scene, since an active participle does not govern when it has past meaning.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r5.claim: Al-waṣīd means either the courtyard or the threshold.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r6.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r6.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r6.claim: Farāran is an accusative cognate accusative because the sense of turning away is fleeing.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r7.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r7.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r7.claim: The Hijazi reading doubles the lām in “they would be filled” for emphasis; the Syrian and ʿAlī readings vocalize the ʿayn with ḍamma.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r8.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r8.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r8.claim: Ruʿb is fear that fills the chest; their terrifying appearance may come from divinely bestowed awe or from long nails, hair, and huge bodies.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r9.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
NASAFI-FULL:v3p6#3/r9.claim: When Muʿāwiya wanted to enter the cave during a Roman campaign, Ibn ʿAbbās warned that even someone better than him would flee; men who entered were killed by a wind.

QASHANI:18:18/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:18:18/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:18:18/r1.claim: The youths seem awake because their eyes, senses, and voluntary animal movements are active, but truly sleep in heedlessness; God turns them between good and virtue and evil and nature.

QASHANI:18:18/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:18:18/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:18:18/r2.claim: Their dog represents the self, its forelegs the powers of anger and desire; it remains awake by the body's threshold, with stronger nobler anger on the right and weaker baser lust on the left.

QASHANI:18:18/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:18:18/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:18:18/r3.claim: An unready observer would flee from their abstract realities and luminous stature, or from their discipline; even an initiate may flee their unity-station in awe of divine majesty.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p132/r15.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p132/r15.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p132/r15.claim: Yaqiẓ means alert; its plurals include ayqāẓ and yiqāẓ, and related masculine and feminine forms are given.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p132/r16.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p132/r16.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p132/r16.claim: Waṣīd means the courtyard, threshold, or door; the cited poem illustrates the term.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r10.speaker: الحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r10.claim: Al-Ḥasan, as cited by Ibn Jinnī, reads وتقلبهم as an accusative verbal noun governed by an omitted verb such as ترى or تشاهد.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r11.speaker: الحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r11.claim: A second report from al-Ḥasan has the verbal noun with ḍamma on yāʾ as a nominative subject, attributed by Abū Ḥātim and Ibn Khalawayh to the Yamani reader.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r12.speaker: عكرمة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r12.claim: ʿIkrima reads وتقلبهم with second-person tāʾ and a light verb, addressing the viewer.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r13.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r13.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r13.claim: The claim that turning prevented earth from wearing clothes or consuming bodies is far-fetched: God could preserve bodies and clothes without turning them.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r14.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r14.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r14.claim: The need to turn the youths to either side is doubtful, since God could preserve their bodies and clothes through the long sleep.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r2.claim: The address in وترى الشمس and وتحسبهم is to anyone who might see the cave.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r3.speaker: author
