ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r3.claim: One view says their eyes were open while asleep, making an observer think they were awake.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r4.speaker: ابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the little visible change and careful preservation could make them look awake; verified open eyes would strengthen that explanation, but the verse does not require it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r5.claim: He takes وتحسبهم أيقاظا as a new statement, though another reading supplies an omitted condition: if you saw them, you would think them awake.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r6.claim: نقلبهم is apparently a new predicate; another view says their turning, especially side to side, made them seem awake.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r7.claim: The majority reading with nūn highlights God’s personal care in turning the youths.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r8.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r8.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī reports ويقلبهم with yāʾ and a doubled lām, understood as God turning them.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r9.speaker: الحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p152/r9.claim: Al-Ḥasan, as cited by al-Ahwāzī, reads ويقلبهم with yāʾ, silent qāf, and a light lām.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r1.claim: He omits conflicting reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Hurayra, Qatāda, Mujāhid, and Ibn ʿAyyāḍ about turning times and counts; such details require reliable revelation, and their contradictory reports cannot all come from it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r10.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r10.claim: Other explanations of الوصيد are the threshold and, from Ibn Jubayr, soil.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r11.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r11.claim: The addressee of لو اطلعت is the same potential observer addressed in ترى الشمس and تحسبهم أيقاظا.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r12.speaker: ابن وثاب والأعمش
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r12.claim: Ibn Waththāb and al-Aʿmash read لو اطلعت with ḍamma on wāw when linking; the majority read its kasra, also reported from Shayba, Abū Jaʿfar, and Nāfiʿ.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r13.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r13.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r13.claim: The terror comes from the awe and majesty God placed around the youths.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r2.claim: He likewise declines reports about the dog’s name and type because such matters are known only through prophetic or scriptural transmission, not reason, and the reports conflict.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r3.claim: كلبهم means the familiar animal; identifying it as a lion, a cook who followed them, or a companion serving as lookout is increasingly implausible.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r4.speaker: أبو عمرو الزاهد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r4.claim: Abū ʿAmr al-Zāhid reports وكالئهم, ‘their guard’; it can still mean the dog because dogs guard people, though a human lookout is also suggested by the posture.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r5.speaker: أبو جعفر الصادق
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r5.claim: Abū Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq reads وكالبهم, meaning the person who owns their dog, like words for an owner of milk or dates.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r6.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r6.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says باسط ذراعيه depicts a past state, since a participle in the past does not govern and possessive attachment makes it definite unless past scene is narrated as present.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r7.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects the claim that past participles cannot govern as non-consensual; al-Kisāʾī, Hishām, and Ibn Maḍāʾ allow it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r8.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses الوصيد as the door; he and Mujāhid and Ibn Jubayr also gloss it as the courtyard.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r9.speaker: قتادة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p153/r9.claim: Qatāda glosses الوصيد as the ground or soil.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p154/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p154/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p154/r1.claim: لوليت means you would turn your face away; فرارا is either a verbal noun for an omitted فررت, for لوليت in the sense of fleeing, or a purpose phrase.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p154/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p154/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p154/r2.claim: رعبا is a second object; parsing it as a transferred specification is unlikely because the verb does not take it as an object, unlike earth producing springs.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p154/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p154/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p154/r3.claim: Explanations of their terrifying appearance based on long hair, nails, pale faces, worn clothes, darkness, or eeriness do not fit the youths’ own estimate of their sleep or the messenger’s reaction; their roomy cave had moving air.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p154/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p154/r4.speaker: ابن عباس والحرميان وأبو حيوة وابن أبي عبلة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p154/r4.claim: These readers pronounce لو اطلعت with a doubled lām and hamza; most of the Seven use a light lām and hamza.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p154/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p154/r5.speaker: أبو جعفر وشيبة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p154/r5.claim: Abū Jaʿfar and Shayba double the lām and replace hamza with yāʾ; al-Zuhrī reads the same replacement with a light lām.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p154/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p154/r6.speaker: أبو جعفر وعيسى
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p154/r6.claim: Abū Jaʿfar and ʿĪsā pronounce the ʿayn of رعبا with ḍamma in this verse; the variant was discussed at Āl ʿImrān.

SAMIN-DURR:18:18#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:18#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:18#2/r1.claim: The alternate reading of رعبا as tamyiz contrasts with its analysis as a second object.

SAMIN-DURR:18:18#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:18#2/r2.speaker: الزهري
SAMIN-DURR:18:18#2/r2.claim: Al-Zuhri reads the lām lightly and substitutes ياء for hamza, a regular sound change.

SAMIN-DURR:18:18#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:18#2/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:18#2/r3.claim: Ibn Kathir and Nafi read لملئت with doubled لام for intensity; Abu Jaafar and Shayba also do so with hamza-to-ياء substitution, while al-Zuhri lightens it.

SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r1.claim: أيقاظ is plural of يقظ; the word has patterns compared with عضد/أعضاد and رجل/رجال.

SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r10.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r10.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r10.claim: فرارا can be a مصدر of the meaning of تولي, a circumstantial “fleeing,” or a purpose object; رعبا is second object or tamyiz.

SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhshari's wording seems to allow يقظ with kasra on قاف.

SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r3.claim: اليقظة means wakefulness, opposite sleep; رقود is plural of راقد, and needs no omitted clause.

SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r4.claim: The common نقلبهم is first-person plural; a ya reading takes God or an angel as subject; al-Hasan has additional light-lām and verbal-noun readings.

SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r5.speaker: الحسن
SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r5.claim: Al-Hasan's nominative وتقلبهم may be a subject with a following locative predicate or an omitted “great sign”; Ikrima has feminine verb with angels as subject.

SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r6.speaker: جعفر الصادق
SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r6.claim: Jaafar al-Sadiq reads كالبهم, meaning the keeper or owner of their dog; Abu Amr al-Zahid transmits وكالئهم, “their guardian.”

SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r7.claim: باسط is an active participle narrating the scene as present; al-Kisa'i allows it to govern.

SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r8.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r8.claim: الوصيد may mean door, threshold, ground, or courtyard; an anonymous poem uses وصيدها.

SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r9.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:18/r9.claim: Most read لو اطلعت with kasra واو by the rule for adjoining sukun; several readers use damma by analogy with واو الضمير.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p143#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p143#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p143#2/r1.claim: Some scholars say the sleepers' eyes remained open to air so they would decay more slowly; a poet compares this to a wolf sleeping with one eye watchful.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p143#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p143#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p143#2/r2.claim: Some early authorities say God turned them from side to side twice a year; Ibn Abbas says the ground would have consumed them if they had not been turned.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p143#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p143#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p143#2/r3.claim: Al-Wasid most correctly means the courtyard or threshold at the entrance, though Ibn Abbas also says door and another view says ground; the word is also used as asid, compare 104:8.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p143#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p143#2/r4.speaker: ابن جريج
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p143#2/r4.claim: Ibn Jurayj says the dog lay at the entrance guarding the youths, in keeping with its nature.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p143#2/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p143#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p143#2/r5.claim: The dog sat outside because angels do not enter a house with a dog, image, ritually impure person, or unbeliever, according to reports; the dog shared the youths' sleep and blessing, showing the benefit of keeping company with the righteous.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p143#2/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p143#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p143#2/r6.claim: The dog was probably one youth's hunting dog; another view says it belonged to the king's cook, who joined their faith.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p143#2/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p143#2/r7.speaker: الحسن البصري
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p143#2/r7.claim: A report transmitted by Ibn Asakir from al-Hasan gives the cave dog the name Qitmir and lists other traditional names and locations, without Ibn Kathir endorsing those details.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p144/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p144/r1.speaker: شعيب الجبائي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p144/r1.claim: Shu'ayb al-Jubba'i reportedly called the dog Hamran, another claimed name.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p144/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p144/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p144/r2.claim: Claims about the dog's color have no value, evidence, or need and are forbidden speculation about the unseen.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p144/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p144/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p144/r3.claim: God placed such awe on the sleepers that anyone who saw them would flee in terror, protecting them from approach or touch until their appointed sleep ended according to God's wisdom and mercy.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p453/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p453/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p453/r1.claim: They seem awake because their eyes are open to the air and they move often, although they are deeply asleep.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p453/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p453/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p453/r2.claim: God turns them from side to side so fresh air reaches every part and prolonged contact with the ground does not harm them.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p453/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p453/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p453/r3.claim: The present participle باسط depicts the dog's continuing past posture; its companionship with the virtuous brings honor even to the dog.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p453/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p453/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p453/r4.claim: The الوصيد is the cave's doorway or courtyard, where dogs customarily lie.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p453/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p453/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p453/r5.claim: God gave the sleepers awe and majesty so that anyone seeing them would flee in terror.

DURR-FULL:v5p365/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p365/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p365/r1.claim: During a campaign near the cave, Muawiya wanted to uncover the sleepers; Ibn Abbas said God had prevented anyone better than him from doing so, and a divinely sent wind drove Muawiya's men out.

DURR-FULL:v5p371/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p371/r10.speaker: ابن عياض
DURR-FULL:v5p371/r10.claim: Ibn Iyad says they were turned over twice each year.

DURR-FULL:v5p371/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p371/r11.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v5p371/r11.claim: Mujahid says they were turned during the nine years, but not during the rest of their sleep.

DURR-FULL:v5p371/r12.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p371/r12.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
DURR-FULL:v5p371/r12.claim: They were turned so that the earth would not consume their flesh.

DURR-FULL:v5p371/r13.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p371/r13.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v5p371/r13.claim: Mujahid gives the dog's name as Qatmur.

DURR-FULL:v5p371/r14.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p371/r14.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v5p371/r14.claim: Hasan gives the dog's name as Qutmir.

DURR-FULL:v5p371/r15.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p371/r15.speaker: ابن جريج
DURR-FULL:v5p371/r15.claim: A scholar rejected the claim that the dog was a lion: it was a red dog brought from home, called Qatmur.

DURR-FULL:v5p371/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p371/r7.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v5p371/r7.claim: Qatada says they looked awake though asleep, during their first sleep.

DURR-FULL:v5p371/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p371/r8.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v5p371/r8.claim: Qatada says they were turned from side to side once each year.

DURR-FULL:v5p371/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p371/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p371/r9.claim: Ibn Abbas says they spent six months on one side and six months on the other.

DURR-FULL:v5p373/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p373/r1.speaker: كثير النواء
DURR-FULL:v5p373/r1.claim: Kathir al-Nawa says the Cave sleepers' dog was yellow.

DURR-FULL:v5p373/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p373/r2.speaker: عبيد
DURR-FULL:v5p373/r2.claim: A trustworthy Kufan man named Ubayd says he saw the dog red like an indigo cloak.

DURR-FULL:v5p373/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p373/r3.speaker: عبيد السواق
DURR-FULL:v5p373/r3.claim: Ubayd al-Sawwaq says the dog was small, with its forelegs extended at the cave's entrance and its ears moving.

DURR-FULL:v5p373/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p373/r4.speaker: عبد الله بن حميد المكي
DURR-FULL:v5p373/r4.claim: The dog received its sustenance by licking its forelegs.

DURR-FULL:v5p373/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p373/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p373/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses الوصيد as the courtyard, and elsewhere as the door.

DURR-FULL:v5p373/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p373/r6.speaker: عطية
DURR-FULL:v5p373/r6.claim: Atiyya explains الوصيد as the courtyard at the cave entrance.

DURR-FULL:v5p373/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p373/r7.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
DURR-FULL:v5p373/r7.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr glosses الوصيد as the bare ground.

DURR-FULL:v5p373/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p373/r8.speaker: ابن جريج
DURR-FULL:v5p373/r8.claim: The dog was positioned as if guarding the cave door.

DURR-FULL:v5p373/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p373/r9.speaker: شهر بن حوشب
DURR-FULL:v5p373/r9.claim: A companion who ignored a warning and looked into the cave had his eyes whiten and hair change; afterward he said the sleepers numbered seven.

BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r1.claim: A continued couplet compares a seeker entering the master's company with a drop entering a shell and becoming a shining pearl.

BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r2.claim: The dog was a shepherd's dog who followed their faith and was named Qitmir; basit depicts a past scene in the present, and its participle can work generally.

BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r3.speaker: الكسائي
BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r3.claim: Al-Kisāʾī, Hishām, and Abū Jaʿfar permit the active participle to govern without restriction; a forearm runs from elbow to the tip of the middle finger.

BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r4.speaker: القاموس
BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r4.claim: Al-waṣīd means the cave's courtyard or threshold; al-Suddī says the cave has no door or threshold and means the dog's place corresponding to a house entrance.

BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r5.speaker: مقاتل
BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r5.claim: A report says ten animals enter Paradise, including the animals of Salih, Abraham, Ishmael, Moses, Jonah, Ezra, Solomon, Bilqis, the Cave youths, and Muhammad; all become rams.

BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r6.speaker: سعدي
BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r6.claim: His verse says the Cave dog joined good people and entered Paradise in a ram's form.

BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r7.speaker: الإمام الثعلبي
BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r7.claim: He transmits that sending blessings on Noah protects one from ticks and carrying the written words about the Cave dog protects one from harm by dogs.

BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r8.speaker: ابن جريج
BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r8.claim: He says the Cave dog was a lion, which can be called a dog, as in the report that a lion ate ʿUtba b. Abī Lahab after the Prophet prayed against him.

BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r9.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r9.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p174#2/r9.claim: Dogs are domestic or Saluqi, named for a Yemeni city with long hunting dogs; al-Zamakhsharī compares badly behaved commoners with Saluqi dogs and notes canine habits.

BURSEVI:v5p174/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p174/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p174/r1.claim: Their open eyes made an observer suppose they were awake; yaqiz and raqid are broken plural forms like the forms for weeping and prostrating in Sūrat Maryam.

BURSEVI:v5p174/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p174/r2.speaker: كشف الأسرار
BURSEVI:v5p174/r2.claim: The youths symbolize spiritual champions: outwardly active in works, inwardly absorbed in divine grace and free of worldly concerns, awake in appearance but inactive within.

BURSEVI:v5p174/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p174/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p174/r3.claim: Angels turned them in sleep so the ground would not consume their bodies; ذات اليمين is an adverbial phrase for the side facing their right.

BURSEVI:v5p174/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p174/r4.speaker: أبو هريرة
BURSEVI:v5p174/r4.claim: He reports that the youths were turned twice each year.

BURSEVI:v5p174/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p174/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
BURSEVI:v5p174/r5.claim: He reports that they were turned once from side to side on Ashura so the earth would not consume their flesh.

BURSEVI:v5p174/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p174/r6.speaker: الإمام
BURSEVI:v5p174/r6.claim: He objects that God could preserve them without turning them; Saʿdī al-Muftī answers that God ordinarily makes things occur through causes.

BURSEVI:v5p174/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p174/r7.speaker: بعض الكبار
BURSEVI:v5p174/r7.claim: Some spiritual masters derive from the verse leaning right while pronouncing negation in the testimony of faith and left during affirmation.

BURSEVI:v5p174/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p174/r8.speaker: التأويلات النجمية
BURSEVI:v5p174/r8.claim: The cited inward reading begins an analogy about the seeker trained directly by God, who must surrender like a corpse before a washer.

BURSEVI:v5p175/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p175/r1.speaker: الإمام اليافعي
BURSEVI:v5p175/r1.claim: One of the dog's ten traits is that when it leaves a place it does not look back, a sign of the sorrowful.

BURSEVI:v5p175/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p175/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p175/r2.claim: If one saw the sleepers, one would flee; الاطلاع means looking over something by direct sight. Fleeing is a verbal noun for turning away, and رعب is fear filling the chest.

BURSEVI:v5p175/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p175/r3.speaker: الكاشفي
BURSEVI:v5p175/r3.claim: He says the youths were terrifying because their eyes were open, their hair and nails had grown, and they lay in a dark, frightening place.

BURSEVI:v5p175/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p175/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
BURSEVI:v5p175/r4.claim: When Muʿāwiya wanted to inspect the cave, Ibn ʿAbbās said even someone better than him had been barred by the verse; Muʿāwiya nevertheless sent men, and a wind burned them or drove them out.

BURSEVI:v5p175/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p175/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p175/r5.claim: The verse's bar means no one can scrutinize them; Muʿāwiya thought the bar applied only before awakening and discovery, while Ibn ʿAbbās knew it applied in every age.

BURSEVI:v5p175/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p175/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p175/r6.claim: The address speaks to the Messenger but signifies anyone in his community, including Muʿāwiya; inspecting extraordinary matters is not accessible to every observer.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r1.claim: Some see the contrast between deep sleep and repeated turning as a display of divine power, but the author considers this unlikely because deep sleep ordinarily has little movement.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r10.claim: Kalbahum most naturally means their actual dog, which has many names and inspired a separate treatise by al-Suyuti.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r11.speaker: كعب الأحبار
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r11.claim: Kaʿb says a dog followed them after they repeatedly drove it away; it reassured them that it loved God's beloved and would guard them.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r12.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r12.claim: Ibn Abbas says it was a shepherd's dog that followed its owner, who had joined the youths' faith.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r13.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r13.claim: Ubayd ibn Umayr says it was either one youth's hunting dog or a sheep dog; keeping a dog for hunting or livestock is permitted, unlike other purposes.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r14.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r14.speaker: ابن عمر
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r14.claim: A hadith in al-Bukhari from Ibn Umar says keeping a dog outside hunting or livestock reduces one's deeds daily by two qirats, or one in another narration.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r15.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r15.speaker: عبيد
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r15.claim: A report from Ubayd says the dog was red like an embroidered cloak; another from Kathir al-Nawwa says yellow, while other accounts say it was spotted.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r16.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r16.speaker: الحسن
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r16.claim: Al-Hasan calls the dog Qitmir; Mujahid calls it Qitmur, while other reports name it Rayyan or Thawr.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r17.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r17.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r17.claim: Ibn Abbas says it was larger than a Qalti and smaller than a Kurdish dog.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r2.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas says they were turned once every six months; Abu Iyad gives a similar report.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r3.claim: Other accounts say they were turned once a year on Ashura, only during the extra nine years, or annually during the first three hundred years but not the additional nine.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r4.speaker: مجاهد
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r4.claim: Mujahid says the turning occurred only in the nine-year addition, not during the preceding period.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r5.speaker: قتادة
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r5.claim: Qatada says they were turned annually during the first three hundred years, but not in the second sleep of nine years.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r6.speaker: الإمام
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r6.claim: The Imam says such timetables cannot be inferred by reason or the Quran and lack an authentic report; the imperfect, intensified verb instead suggests repeated turning.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r7.speaker: الطيبي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r7.claim: Al-Tibi suggests the turning clause is circumstantial based on al-Zajjaj's explanation, but the author finds that analysis unconvincing.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r8.claim: The readings include yuqallibuhum with yāʾ, whose subject may be God or an angel; al-Hasan also has a lighter form, while Ibn Jinni reports the verbal-noun reading taqallubahum.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r9.speaker: ابن جني
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224#2/r9.claim: Ibn Jinni parses taqallubahum as an accusative verbal noun governed by an omitted “you see,” or as an initial noun with a following predicate; Ikrima reads a light verb addressed to the observer.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224/r1.claim: The default hasabtum has an open sīn; Nafiʿ, Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, and al-Kisai read it with kasra, meaning “you think,” as in the earlier address.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224/r2.claim: The statement may be a fresh report, or it may omit “if you saw them,” yielding “you would think them awake.”

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224/r3.speaker: الكشف
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224/r3.claim: Al-Kashf parses ayqazan as the plural of yaqiz, with either kasra or damma on qaf, comparing each form to its corresponding plural pattern.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224/r4.speaker: القاموس
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224/r4.claim: The Qamus records both qaf vowels in yaqiz and yaqizān; open eyes create the main impression of wakefulness.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224/r5.speaker: ابن عطية
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224/r5.claim: Ibn Atiyya says an observer might infer wakefulness from their preserved appearance and lack of normal sleeping slackness even with closed eyes; reliably established open eyes would make the impression clearer.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p224/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224/r6.speaker: الزجاج
ALUSI-FULL:v15p224/r6.claim: Al-Zajjaj says frequent turning explains why they seemed awake, but the author objects that this does not fit the explicit statement that they were asleep.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r1.speaker: عبيد
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r1.claim: Ubayd reportedly saw the dog as a small “Zini” animal, which al-Suyuti explains as Chinese; al-Khazini likewise interprets the Qalti as Chinese.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r10.claim: Basit dhiraʿayhi means stretching the two forelegs; the participle governs its object because the narration depicts a past scene, or because some grammarians allow it in any tense.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r11.claim: Al-wasid means the cave's doorway or passage; reports from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Atiyya gloss it as the area in front, while others say threshold or its adjacent ground.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r12.speaker: ابن جبير
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r12.claim: Ibn Jubayr's reported gloss of wasid as ṣaʿid is judged unsound.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r13.speaker: ابن جريج
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r13.claim: The dog lay at the entrance to guard the cave; another report says it slept on one ear as the youths turned and switched ears when they turned the other way.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r14.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r14.speaker: عبد الله بن حميد المكي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r14.claim: A report from Abd Allah ibn Humayd al-Makki says the dog lived by licking its forelegs, suggesting it did not sleep through the entire period.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r15.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r15.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r15.claim: Ittalaʿta means to come upon something by direct sight and inspection.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r16.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r16.speaker: ابن وثاب والأعمش
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r16.claim: Ibn Waththab and al-Aʿmash read ittaṭlaʿ with a damma on wāw by analogy with a pronoun wāw before a still letter; Shayba and Abu Jaʿfar also transmit it.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r2.claim: Some say kalb means lion, a possible dictionary sense; a Prophetic supplication against an unbeliever was fulfilled by a lion, but that does not fit the verse's plain wording.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r3.speaker: ابن جريج
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r3.claim: Ibn Jurayj asked a learned man whether the dog was a lion; the man swore it was a red dog called Qitmura.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r4.claim: More remote claims identify the dog as a human cook or attendant, or one of the youths stationed as a lookout.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r5.speaker: أبو عمرو الزاهدي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r5.claim: Abu Amr al-Zahidi records a reading kalibahum with hamza and alif from “to guard,” which could mean a human sentinel; the canonical reading still points to a dog.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r6.speaker: جعفر الصادق
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r6.claim: Jaʿfar al-Sadiq reads kalibahum with a doubled noun pattern, meaning the owner of their dog, like someone described as owning milk or dates.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r7.speaker: خالد بن معدان
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r7.claim: Khalid ibn Maʿdan says the only beasts in Paradise are the cave dog and Balaam's donkey; other lists include Salih's camel and Ishmael's ram but lack reliable support.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r8.claim: An account understood from al-Tirmidhi's wording appears to affirm horses in Paradise, while claims about other animals have no report one can rely on.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p225/r9.claim: Some Shiʿites name sons “Dog of Ali” and hope for salvation by analogy; a popular poem celebrates the cave dog and dog of Ali, which the author answers with a joke about Ali's own dog.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p227#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227#2/r1.claim: Defenders answer that people waking may not notice their changed condition; the messenger's ignorance does not rule out others noticing it, and he may initially have spoken before realizing the duration.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p227#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227#2/r2.claim: Another response addresses the Prophet: frightening changes and an eerie setting could have developed after the sleepers awoke and sent their messenger into town.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p227#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227#2/r3.claim: The author finds these counterarguments weak; the best explanation is awe God placed on them, with any grown hair or nails not reaching a startling length.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p227#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227#2/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227#2/r4.claim: Some commentators say God never altered their appearance at all, preserving a clear sign; if the address is to the Prophet, their terrifying appearance must have lasted until revelation.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p227#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227#2/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas recounts that during a campaign with Muawiya near the Roman lands, Muawiya wanted to inspect the cave, but Ibn Abbas said God had barred it even to someone better than him, namely the Prophet.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p227#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227#2/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227#2/r6.claim: Muawiya insisted and sent men inside; God sent a wind that drove them out of the cave.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p227#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227#2/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227#2/r7.claim: One explanation says Muawiya thought their condition had changed; another says he simply wanted to learn about them if possible.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p227/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227/r1.claim: Lawallayta means turning away and showing them one's back; fararan may be an emphatic verbal noun, stand for an omitted verb, describe one's state, or give the reason for retreating.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p227/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227/r2.claim: Fear filling someone is a familiar metaphor for its intensity; ruʿban may be a second object or a specification converted from the subject.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p227/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227/r3.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227/r3.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects deriving ruʿban from an object as in “the earth burst into springs,” since the verb here would otherwise govern a direct object.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p227/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227/r4.claim: The author says the cause of terror was the awe and majesty God cast upon the youths; others attribute it to long hair and nails, yellow faces, worn clothes, or a dark, desolate cave.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p227/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227/r5.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v15p227/r5.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects the bodily-change and desolate-place explanations: the youths themselves did not recognize changes, the messenger noticed only altered landmarks, and the spacious cave was not desolate.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p228#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228#2/r1.claim: An anecdote about Moses teaches that the first cure worked because he went to the plant through God, while the later attempt relied on himself.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p228#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228#2/r2.claim: Alusi calls it objectionable for a mystic to claim he would not flee or feel terror if he saw the sleepers.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p228#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228#2/r3.claim: The excuse that the speaker meant he was like an unafraid child does not remove the impropriety; Alusi likens it to an irreverent claim about God's knowledge of the unseen and invokes Umar's advice to speak understandably.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p228#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228#2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس، الحرميان، أبو حيوة، ابن أبي عبلة
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228#2/r4.claim: These readers intensify the lām and retain the hamza in ولملئت.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p228#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228#2/r5.speaker: أبو جعفر، شيبة
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228#2/r5.claim: They intensify the lām and change the hamza to yāʾ in the reading of ولملئت.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p228#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228#2/r6.speaker: الزهري
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228#2/r6.claim: Al-Zuhri reads with a light lām and the hamza changed to yāʾ.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p228#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228#2/r7.speaker: أبو جعفر، عيسى
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228#2/r7.claim: Abu Jaʿfar and ʿIsa read ruʿuban with ḍamma on the ʿayn.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p228/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228/r1.speaker: شهر بن حوشب
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228/r1.claim: A man who insisted on looking into the cave emerged with whitened eyes and changed hair, and said the sleepers numbered seven; the report could support their present existence.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p228/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228/r2.speaker: السهيلي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228/r2.claim: Al-Suhayli transmits that some people held the sleepers still existed in the cave.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p228/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas denied their bones remained, saying they had disappeared more than three hundred years earlier when he passed the cave with Habib b. Maslama; the report is from Ikrima.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p228/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228/r4.claim: Alusi inclines to their no longer existing and, when alive, not remaining in the described state; the verse reports their condition then and addresses no particular individual.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p228/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228/r5.claim: A report attributed through Ibn Mardawayh to Ibn Abbas says the Prophet called the Companions of the Cave helpers of the Mahdi; even if sound, it does not prove they exist today in that state.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p228/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p228/r6.claim: If the Prophet is treated as specifically addressed, the flight-and-terror consequence is explained by ordinary human nature; another proposal distinguishes God's disclosure to him from an unaided personal sighting.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r1.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r1.claim: The cave dog can symbolize their souls, asleep and inactive in works, or souls so disciplined that circumstances obey and protect them from harm.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r2.speaker: جعفر الصادق
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259#2/r2.claim: A vision of their awe-inspiring divine robe would make an observer flee in terror, like Moses fleeing his transformed staff; the flight is really from God's majesty displayed in that mirror. This is reported from Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p259/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259/r3.speaker: ابن عطاء
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259/r3.claim: Their apparent wakefulness and sleep signify that their bodies remain among people while their spirits abide with God; Ibn ʿAṭāʾ describes them as beyond time and place, alive and dead, asleep yet alert in the divine presence.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p259/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259/r4.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259/r4.claim: Turning them right and left can mean moving them between worlds; Ibn ʿAṭāʾ says contraction and expansion or gathering and separation, another says annihilation and subsistence or unveiling and concealment, and another compares their surrender to a corpse in a washer's hands.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p259/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259/r5.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259/r5.claim: Abū Bakr al-Warrāq says companionship and proximity to the righteous are a great gain even across different species, as shown by God's mention of the dog alongside the cave companions.

ELMALILI:18:15-18/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:15-18/r12.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:15-18/r12.claim: Although asleep, the companions' eyes were open, making them look awake.

ELMALILI:18:15-18/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:15-18/r13.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:15-18/r13.claim: God turned them from side to side, while their dog lay at the cave entrance with its forelegs outstretched; their fearful appearance made discovery impossible.

ELMALILI:18:15-18/r14.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:15-18/r14.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:15-18/r14.claim: Anyone who saw them would flee, filled with terror; their awe prevented anyone from learning their condition.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p280/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p280/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p280/r1.claim: This continuation presents the sleepers’ appearance as a lesson in their honor and God’s power, astonishing anyone who might see them.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p280/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p280/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p280/r2.claim: One explanation is that their eyes were open, making their condition resemble wakefulness while differing from ordinary sleep.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p280/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p280/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p280/r3.claim: The imperfect taḥsabuhum indicates that the appearance of wakefulness recurred over a long period.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p280/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p280/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p280/r4.claim: Aiqāẓ is the plural of yaqiz, with either kasra or ḍamma on the qāf; ruqūd is the plural of rāqid.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p280/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p280/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p280/r5.claim: Taqlīb means changing an object’s position from its exterior to its interior; the Qur’an uses it for someone turning over his hands at 18:42.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p280/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p280/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p280/r6.claim: God turned them from right to left and back, treating them like living, wakeful people; this may have helped preserve their bodies.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p280/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p280/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p280/r7.claim: The imperfect verb conveys repeated renewal throughout the narrated period; it does not require that the sleepers remained in this state at revelation.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r1.claim: The dog stayed at the entrance with forelegs extended, unlike the sleepers who were turned; its fixed position marks their special care and honor.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r2.claim: Al-waṣīd is the cave entrance, compared to a door because it can be shut.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r3.claim: Because the dog was not turned, their turning was not needed to prevent decay but was an honor; it is also possible they survived while the dog died and became bones.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r4.claim: The address is generic and describes someone seeing them before they awoke; the text does not say this remained their state at revelation.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r5.claim: The observer would mistake the group in a cave for bandits, since caves sheltered highwaymen, and flee from fear of their danger rather than their appearance or death.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r6.speaker: تأبط شرا
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r6.claim: Taʾabbaṭa Sharran’s verse evokes an obstructed cave and flight from dangerous men, supporting the bandit interpretation of the observer’s fear.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r7.claim: Iṭṭilāʿ is literally climbing to look down, then conventionally means seeing what others cannot; the verse’s warning is not fear of dead bodies.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p281/r8.claim: Al-Kashshāf suggests, on Ibn ʿAbbās’s authority, that the address targets the Prophet; Ibn Ashur says this is not sound.

TABATABAI:18:26#3/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:26#3/r1.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:18:26#3/r1.claim: The Qummi narration says they sleep six months on each side, turn twice yearly, and their dog lies at the cave entrance.

TABATABAI:18:26#3/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:26#3/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:26#3/r2.claim: The author says no known cave on earth contains sleepers in this state, and that the narration conflicts with the verse’s apparent account of the crowd’s debate and the youths’ fate.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#29/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#29/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TABATABAI:18:9-26#29/r3.claim: During a campaign with Muawiya near Roman territory, Ibn Abbas forbids opening the cave because the Quran says an observer would flee in terror; Muawiya sends men anyway, and a wind drives them back.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#30/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#30/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#30/r4.claim: Although commentators widely accept this report, the known cave near the strait at Ephesus does not fit its description, and the fear verse describes their state before awakening, not afterward.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#31/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#31/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
TABATABAI:18:9-26#31/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas passed a cave with companions and found bones; another man identified them as the Cave youths, and Ibn Abbas answered that their bones would have decayed after more than three hundred years.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#31/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#31/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TABATABAI:18:9-26#31/r2.claim: Another account has Ibn Abbas tell a campaigner that the youths’ bones would have decayed after more than three hundred years; this chronology places the story early in or before the Common Era and conflicts with most reports.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#31/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#31/r7.speaker: أبو جعفر عليه السلام
TABATABAI:18:9-26#31/r7.claim: A report from al-Baqir says the warning about looking into the cave was addressed to believers among themselves, not specifically to the Prophet, and describes their actual condition.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r10.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r10.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r10.claim: The cave story circulated in detailed reports from al-Qummī, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid, Ibn Isḥāq, Wahb ibn Munabbih, and al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, among others.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r1.claim: The transmitted accounts disagree even on major features, while reports about dates, rulers, lineage, appearance, names, and the title أصحاب الرقيم diverge still more.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r2.claim: One cause is the story’s prominence among People of the Book: Quraysh learned it from them, and its Christian images and monuments spread it widely, so communities reshaped it to fit their beliefs.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r3.claim: A second cause is Muslims’ broad collection of outside reports, especially through converts such as Wahb ibn Munabbih and Kaʿb al-Aḥbār; later transmitters treated such material as prophetic reports.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r4.claim: The Qurʾān selects key lessons that serve guidance instead of supplying a complete historical account; it is a book of guidance, not history.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r1.claim: The Qurʾān omits names, ancestry, birth, upbringing, occupations, social standing, dates, rulers, cities, persecutors, and the dog’s identity because guidance does not depend on them; historians and early exegetes filled these gaps, producing divergent accounts.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r4.claim: The narrative presents the youths sleeping in the cave with their dog for the stated long period, protected by the cave’s position and God’s care.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r1.speaker: أهل الرواية والتاريخ
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r1.claim: Most historians date the story between Jesus and Muḥammad; it is absent from the two Testaments, though some Muslim reports say Quraysh heard it from Jews, while Christians preserved it extensively.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r2.claim: Christian accounts resemble Ibn Isḥāq’s report from Ibn ʿAbbās in some respects but differ from Muslims on the number of sleepers, whether they had a dog, and the length of their sleep.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r4.claim: After centuries as a ruined, forgotten site, Jordanian excavation uncovered Rujayb; the author considers its archaeological signs and some Muslim reports the strongest fit for the Qurʾānic cave.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r1.claim: Amman stands on the site of Philadelphia, a major and beautiful city before Islam that remained under Roman control from the early second century until the Muslim conquest.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r2.claim: Other proposed locations include a cave on Mount Qāsiyūn near Damascus, one at Petra, a Scandinavian cave with seven uncorrupted Roman-looking bodies, and a cave near Nakhchivan.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r3.claim: No evidence identifies any proposed cave as the Qurʾānic one; the Scandinavian and Caucasus claims conflict with the story’s Roman setting and the limits of Roman power.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#9/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#9/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#9/r3.claim: Aiqāẓ means awake people and ruqūd sleepers; the phrasing hints that they slept with eyes open.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#9/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#9/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#9/r4.claim: God turned them from side to side to prevent decay of their bodies and clothes and loss of bodily strength from prolonged stillness.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#9/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#9/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#9/r5.claim: Al-waṣīd is the courtyard or threshold; the dog lay at the cave entrance and remained with them throughout their stay.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#9/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#9/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#9/r6.claim: Their appearance was so frightening that an observer would flee in anticipation of harm and be filled with dread spreading through the body.

ASAD-NOTES:18:18#n21/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:18:18#n21/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:18:18#n21/r1.claim: An accidental onlooker would sense the Cave youths' awe-inspiring aura and recognize them as God's elect, as classical commentators explain.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Their appearance of wakefulness protected them: a passerby might think they were merely resting and thus hesitate to harm them.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: God turned them from side to side to preserve their health and prevent stiffness during the long sleep, like an affectionate mother turning a child in a cradle.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The dog guarded the entrance in a sentinel's unusual sleeping posture, deterring people and wild animals from entering.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The spectacle was meant to frighten onlookers away and protect the youths; their cave and forest shelter contrasted with the insecurity of rulers guarded in castles.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:18/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:18/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:18/r1.claim: The sleeping youths appeared awake in a dark, remote cave; their dog lay at the entrance as if guarding them, perhaps to protect against wild animals.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:18/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:18/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:18/r2.claim: Their changed appearance, including long hair and beards, would frighten onlookers; God turned them from side to side to preserve their bodies during the long sleep.

QIRAAT-ER:18:18:2#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:18:18:2#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:18:18:2#1/r1.claim: Kasra on sīn contrasts with standard fatḥa as a dialectal Form I vowel variant.

QIRAAT-ER:18:18:29#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:18:18:29#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:18:18:29#1/r1.claim: Replacing hamza with yāʾ removes the glottal stop as a dialectal pronunciation variant.

QIRAAT-ER:18:18:29#2/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:18:18:29#2/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:18:18:29#2/r1.claim: Geminating lām gives Form II passive and intensifies the sense of being filled.

QIRAAT-ER:18:18:29#3/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:18:18:29#3/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:18:18:29#3/r1.claim: This form combines Form II intensification through geminated lām with hamza avoidance by yāʾ.

QIRAAT-ER:18:18:31#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:18:18:31#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:18:18:31#1/r1.claim: Ḍamma on ʿayn inserts a vowel within the same noun without changing meaning.

STUDYQURAN:18:18/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r1.speaker: R, Z
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r1.claim: Their seeming awake despite sleeping may reflect open eyes or turning once or twice yearly.

STUDYQURAN:18:18/r10.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r10.speaker: Q, Th
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r10.claim: Some say the youths encountered the dog while fleeing, tried to chase it away, and it was miraculously enabled to speak.

STUDYQURAN:18:18/r11.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r11.speaker: Q, R, Th
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r11.claim: The speaking dog reportedly said it loved God’s lovers and would keep watch while they slept.

STUDYQURAN:18:18/r12.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r12.speaker: R
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r12.claim: Another account says a sheepdog and its shepherd followed the youths.

STUDYQURAN:18:18/r13.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r13.speaker: Ṭ, Z
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r13.claim: Some identify kalb as a companion’s name, perhaps their cook or dog keeper; another reading kālib yields dog keeper, and “paws” becomes “arms.”

STUDYQURAN:18:18/r14.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r14.speaker: Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r14.claim: Waṣīd translated as threshold can also mean the cave’s door or entrance, or the earth or dust in front of it.

STUDYQURAN:18:18/r15.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r15.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r15.claim: The verse addresses the Prophet; God’s fearsome appearance for the youths kept anyone from touching or disturbing them as they slept.

STUDYQURAN:18:18/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r2.claim: Their appearance may indicate a state between ordinary waking and sleep.

STUDYQURAN:18:18/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r3.speaker: Prophet
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r3.claim: A well-known hadith says that people are asleep and awaken when they die, associating worldly wakefulness with sleep and death with full awakening.

STUDYQURAN:18:18/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r4.claim: Sleep and waking can symbolize death and resurrection, as in the verse describing God taking souls at night and resurrecting them by day.

STUDYQURAN:18:18/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r5.claim: Sleep is an intermediate barzakh: the soul is taken while one remains alive, making sleep a minor death and waking a resurrection.

STUDYQURAN:18:18/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r6.claim: The Cave story can allegorize barzakh, the interval between individual death and universal resurrection, as well as prove resurrection.

STUDYQURAN:18:18/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r7.speaker: Su
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r7.claim: From a Sufi perspective, the youths’ turning represents alternation between annihilation and subsistence in God.

STUDYQURAN:18:18/r8.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r8.speaker: Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r8.claim: God turned them to prevent the earth from covering and eventually consuming their bodies.

STUDYQURAN:18:18/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r9.speaker: Th
STUDYQURAN:18:18/r9.claim: Some commentators say the dog served as their hunting animal.
